chunks: As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād, from al-Ḥalabī, who said:
Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: “The free man does not confer iḥṣān upon the bondwoman, nor does the bondsman upon the free woman.”

So this report does not contradict what we presented earlier of the reports stating that the bondwoman does confer iḥṣān, because the meaning in this report is that the free man does not confer upon her the iḥṣān such that, if she were to commit zina, rajm would become obligatory upon her, just as if a free woman were under him and committed zina, rajm would be obligatory upon her. That is because the hadd of the bondsman and bondwoman, when they commit zina, is half the hadd of the free person, namely fifty lashes, and they are not stoned in this respect. Likewise, his saying, “nor does the bondsman [confer iḥṣān upon] the free woman,” means that the free woman does not confer iḥṣān upon him such that rajm would become obligatory upon him. According to this interpretation, there is no contradiction between the reports.

key_terms.الرَّجْمُ: stoning as the legal penalty in the case of fully established iḥṣān
key_terms.خَمْسُونَ جَلْدَةً: fifty lashes, the reduced hadd for the enslaved person in this context
key_terms.يُحْصِنُ: to confer iḥṣān, meaning the protected marital status relevant to zina rulings

ai.seo_question: Does marriage between a free person and an enslaved person establish iḥṣān for the hadd of zina?
ai.summary: This report discusses the legal meaning of iḥṣān in the rulings of zina for free and enslaved spouses. It explains that a marriage between a free person and an enslaved person does not produce the level of iḥṣān that would entail rajm, since the hadd for the enslaved man or woman remains half that of the free person.
